title: Using kinetic energy and energy changes

prerequisites.provenance_note: The immediate handoff from 9702_t05_cm03_l05 is authoritative for kinetic-energy prior learning. No controlled Topic 5 course-module lesson map exists in this checkout, so the delegated lesson title and official use outcome 9702_t05_m02_o04 bound new learning.

prior_knowledge_summary: Kinetic energy is energy that an object has because of its motion.
The previous lesson derived E_K = 1/2 mv^2 and Delta E_K = 1/2 m(v^2 - u^2).
Work done by a resultant force changes kinetic energy.
Work done is the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force.
Energy is conserved: energy may be transferred between stores or dissipated, but the total energy of a closed system does not disappear.
The change in gravitational potential energy in a uniform field is given by Delta E_P = mg Delta h.
Mass is measured in kg, speed in m s^-1 and energy in J.
new_learning: Select and use E_K = 1/2 mv^2 in direct and reverse calculations.
Use Delta E_K = 1/2 m(v^2 - u^2) with a consistent final-minus-initial sign.
Compare kinetic energies efficiently when mass, speed or both change.
Carry kinetic energy through multi-stage energy ledgers that include gravitational transfer and dissipation.
not_yet_taught: elastic strain energy and spring calculations

blocks.title: Why does doubling speed feel like much more than doubling?
content: Imagine the same trolley rolling at 2.0 m s^-1 and then at 4.0 m s^-1. Its mass has not changed, yet the faster trolley is much harder to stop.
A tempting prediction is that twice the speed means twice the energy. The physics test is to connect the stopping work to the motion and see what the speed actually does.

figure.purpose: Create the need for a squared speed relationship
figure.brief: Landscape white-paper teacher sketch of two identical trolleys at 2.0 m s^-1 and 4.0 m s^-1 approaching equal rough stopping strips. Show prediction bubbles for twice or four times the energy, but do not reveal which is correct.
figure.alt_text: Two identical trolleys approach rough strips at two different speeds, prompting a prediction about their energies.

blocks.title: Bring forward the kinetic-energy model
blocks.accepted_definition: energy that an object has because of its motion
content: From Lesson 5, kinetic energy is energy that an object has because of its motion.
The formula to remember and now use fluently is E_K = 1/2 mv^2. E_K is kinetic energy in J, m is mass in kg and v is speed in m s^-1.
Speed is used, not velocity direction. Reversing direction without changing speed does not change kinetic energy because v is squared.

figure.purpose: Connect the controlled definition, formula, symbols and SI units
figure.brief: Landscape white-paper formula map centred on E_K = one half m v squared, with arrows to kinetic energy in J, mass in kg and speed in m s^-1. Include two equal-speed arrows in opposite directions leading to equal kinetic-energy boxes.
figure.alt_text: A formula map links kinetic energy to mass and the square of speed and shows that direction does not affect it.

blocks.title: A short check on where the formula came from
content: Lesson 5 derived the formula. Recall the route for a quick check: an object of mass m speeds up from rest to speed v under a constant resultant force F through displacement s. The work done is W = Fs and Newton's second law gives F = ma, so W = mas.
For constant acceleration from rest, v^2 = 2as, so as = v^2/2. Substituting gives W = m(v^2/2) = 1/2 mv^2.

Here W is work in J, F is resultant force in N, s is displacement in m, m is mass in kg, a is acceleration in m s^-2, and u and v are initial and final speeds in m s^-1. The work done on the object becomes its kinetic-energy gain. This recalled route is a check on the formula, not new derivation content.

figure.purpose: Show every causal and algebraic step in the derivation
figure.brief: Landscape white-paper linked-stage derivation: force through distance gives W = Fs; F = ma gives W = mas; motion from rest gives v squared = 2as; substitution leads to W = one half m v squared. Mark the carried quantity as = kinetic-energy gain.
figure.alt_text: Work, force and constant-acceleration equations combine step by step to derive kinetic energy.

blocks.title: Mass is linear, speed is squared
content: For a 3.0 kg delivery cart moving at 2.0 m s^-1, E_K = 1/2 x 3.0 x 2.0^2 = 6.0 J.
At 4.0 m s^-1, the same cart has E_K = 1/2 x 3.0 x 4.0^2 = 24 J. Doubling speed multiplies kinetic energy by four.
A different cart of mass 6.0 kg moving at 2.0 m s^-1 has 12 J. Doubling mass only doubles kinetic energy. A ratio is often shorter than two full calculations: E_2/E_1 = (m_2/m_1)(v_2/v_1)^2.
Check the first comparison: 24 J / 6.0 J = 4, matching (4.0/2.0)^2.

figure.purpose: Contrast linear mass dependence with squared speed dependence
figure.brief: Landscape white-paper comparison table for 3.0 kg at 2.0 m s^-1 giving 6.0 J, 3.0 kg at 4.0 m s^-1 giving 24 J, and 6.0 kg at 2.0 m s^-1 giving 12 J. Highlight x4 for doubled speed and x2 for doubled mass.
figure.alt_text: Three cart cases show that doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy while doubling mass doubles it.

blocks.title: Energy change means final minus initial
content: A 750 kg test vehicle slows from 18 m s^-1 to 10 m s^-1. Write the boundary first: Delta E_K = E_K,final - E_K,initial.
The negative sign means the vehicle's kinetic energy decreases by 8.40 x 10^4 J. It does not mean kinetic energy itself is negative.
Independent check: E_K,initial = 1.215 x 10^5 J and E_K,final = 3.75 x 10^4 J. Their difference is -8.40 x 10^4 J.

figure.purpose: Teach signed final-minus-initial energy change and a second-route check
figure.brief: Landscape white-paper before-and-after energy ledger for a 750 kg vehicle slowing from 18 to 10 m s^-1. Show separate initial and final kinetic-energy boxes, subtraction final minus initial, and a note that negative Delta E_K means a decrease.
figure.alt_text: A before-and-after ledger calculates a negative kinetic-energy change for a slowing vehicle.

blocks.title: Use kinetic energy inside an energy ledger
content: A 2.0 kg trolley starts from rest and descends through a vertical height of 1.5 m. During the motion, 5.4 J is dissipated. The gravitational potential energy decrease is mg Delta h = 2.0 x 9.81 x 1.5 = 29.43 J. Here g = 9.81 m s^-2 is gravitational field strength expressed as acceleration, and Delta h is the vertical height change in m.
Energy accounting gives final kinetic energy = 29.43 - 5.4 = 24.03 J. Now use 24.03 = 1/2 x 2.0 x v^2, so v = sqrt(24.03) = 4.90 m s^-1.
Check the ledger: 24.03 J kinetic plus 5.4 J dissipated equals 29.43 J transferred from gravitational potential energy.

A common idea is to write mgh = 1/2 mv^2 automatically. That feels natural because falling often speeds an object up, but it fails when energy is dissipated or when the object already has kinetic energy. Write the complete before-and-after ledger first.

figure.purpose: Combine prior gravitational-energy knowledge with current kinetic-energy use and expose omitted losses
figure.brief: Landscape white-paper energy flow ledger: 29.43 J gravitational potential decrease splits into 24.03 J final kinetic energy and 5.4 J dissipated. Beside it show the speed rearrangement and the exact sum check.
figure.alt_text: An energy ledger includes both final kinetic energy and dissipated energy for a descending trolley.

blocks.title: A reliable route for kinetic-energy problems
content: First decide whether you need one kinetic energy, a final-minus-initial change, a ratio or an energy ledger. Then convert mass to kg and use speed in m s^-1.
Use E_K = 1/2 mv^2. Square the speed before multiplying. For reverse questions, isolate v^2 before taking the positive square root because speed is a magnitude.
Finish by checking the unit J, the sign of a change, the squared-speed effect and any before-and-after energy balance.
